To mitigate the risk, it is recommended to enforce multifactor authentication for all remote access to ICS networks and devices. Additionally, changing all passwords to ICS/SCADA devices and systems on a consistent schedule is advised. Lastly, leveraging a properly installed continuous OT monitoring solution can help in early detection and response to similar threats in the future.

Immediate action is required to ensure the security and integrity of the affected systems and to prevent potential further damage. A thorough investigation, remediation, and recovery plan should be developed and executed promptly.

Title: Technical Incident Report - Unauthorized Access and Potential Exploitation of Vulnerabilities in VMware Products

This report outlines an incident involving potential unauthorized access and exploitation of vulnerabilities in VMware products, attributed to malicious cyber actors, likely advanced persistent threat (APT) actors.

The incident is centered around four identified vulnerabilities: CVE-2022-22954, CVE-2022-22960, CVE-2022-22972, and CVE-2022-22973. VMware released updates for these vulnerabilities on April 6, 2022. Subsequently, on April 14, 2022, and April 15, 2022, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2022-22954 and CVE-2022-22960, respectively, to its catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities. On May 5, 2022, and May 6, 2022, federal agencies were required to apply updates for CVE-2022-22954 and CVE-2022-22960, respectively.

The identified vulnerabilities allow malicious actors to trigger a server-side template injection. This could potentially result in remote code execution (RCE) or escalation of privileges to root. The impact of such exploitation could be significant, potentially leading to unauthorized access, data theft, and system disruption.

To mitigate this risk, it is recommended that affected organizations apply the updates for CVE-2022-22954 and CVE-2022-22960 as soon as possible. As a temporary measure, it is also advisable to remove the affected software from their network until the updates can be applied.

This incident underscores the importance of timely software updates and vigilance in the face of known exploited vulnerabilities. Continuous monitoring and swift response are crucial in mitigating risks posed by advanced persistent threat actors. Further investigation is ongoing to determine the extent of the breach, if any, and to identify the specific tactics, techniques, and procedures used by the malicious actors.

This report details an incident involving potential exploitation of vulnerabilities in VMware products by malicious cyber actors, suspected to be advanced persistent threat (APT) actors.

The incident centers around four identified vulnerabilities: CVE-2022-22954, CVE-2022-22960, CVE-2022-22972, and CVE-2022-22973. On April 6, 2022, VMware released updates for these vulnerabilities. Subsequently, on April 14, 2022, and April 15, 2022, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2022-22954 and CVE-2022-22960, respectively, to its catalog of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities. On May 5, 2022, and May 6, 2022, federal agencies were mandated to apply updates for CVE-2022-22954 and CVE-2022-22960, respectively.

The identified vulnerabilities allow malicious actors to perform a server-side template injection, potentially resulting in remote code execution (RCE) or escalation of privileges to root. The implications of such exploitation could be severe, potentially leading to unauthorized access, data theft, and system disruption.

To mitigate this risk, it is recommended that affected organizations apply the updates for CVE-2022-22954 and CVE-2022-22960 promptly. As a temporary measure, it is also advisable to remove the affected software from their network until the updates can be applied.

This incident underscores the significance of timely software updates and vigilance in the face of known exploited vulnerabilities. Continuous monitoring and swift response are essential in countering the threats posed by advanced persistent threat actors. Ongoing investigation aims to ascertain the extent of the breach, if any, and to identify the specific tactics, techniques, and procedures employed by the malicious actors.

Title: Technical Incident Report - Unauthorized Data Exfiltration and Evidence Deletion

On April 12, two distinct cyber threat actors, Threat Actor 1 (TA1) and Threat Actor 2 (TA2), were identified as having infiltrated a public-facing server running VMWare Workspace ONE Access. The initial point of entry for both actors was a vulnerability identified as CVE 2022-22960.

TA1 utilized a malicious shell script, and TA2 deployed a Dingo J-spy webshell, both known malicious tools in the cyber threat landscape. Additionally, TA1 is suspected to have executed a malicious Bash script during the course of the incident.

The actors engaged in a series of tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) that are commonly observed in targeted attacks. These included initial access (T1071.001), command and control (C2) (T1068), execution (TA0004), persistence (T1070), privilege escalation (TA0005), and lateral movement (T1573.001).

The primary objective of the attackers appeared to be sensitive data exfiltration, as well as the deletion of evidence of their compromise. The Freemarker application on the affected server was targeted for data extraction, and signs of deleted logs and system files indicate an attempt to cover their tracks.

The targeted sector remains unknown at this stage of the investigation. However, the sophistication of the attack methods suggests a well-resourced and organized threat actor.

Upon discovering the incident, immediate actions were taken to patch the vulnerability (CVE 2022-22960) and implement security best practices as mitigations to prevent further intrusions. A thorough investigation is underway to comprehensively understand the extent and impact of the breach, as well as to identify any additional compromised systems or sensitive data.

Title: Cyber Incident Report - PRC State-Sponsored Attacks since 2020

The investigation has uncovered a persistent cyber threat targeting public and private sector organizations, with a focus on major telecommunications companies, network service providers, and entities within the Defense Industrial Base (DIB) and critical infrastructure (CI). The actor behind these attacks has been identified as People's Republic of China (PRC) state-sponsored cyber actors.

The primary tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) used by the actor have remained consistent since 2020, with the attacks primarily exploiting Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs). No specific malware has been identified in this incident.

The impact of these attacks is yet to be fully assessed, but the potential for data breaches, system disruptions, and intellectual property theft is significant. It is crucial to emphasize the need for immediate action to mitigate the risks.

Recommended mitigations include applying patches as soon as they become available, disabling unnecessary ports and protocols, replacing end-of-life infrastructure, and implementing a centralized patch management system.

Given the ongoing nature of these attacks and the sensitive sectors targeted, it is imperative that organizations prioritize cybersecurity measures to protect their assets and maintain business continuity. Continuous monitoring and threat intelligence are key to staying ahead of these threats.

Title: Technical Incident Report - State-Sponsored APT Attack Leveraging Log4Shell Vulnerability

In the month of December 2021, a series of cyber attacks were identified, originating from state-sponsored Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) actors. The attacks targeted organizations with affected systems, exploiting the Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228) in public-facing VMware Horizon and Unified Access Gateway (UAG) servers.

The APT actors successfully exploited the Log4Shell vulnerability, also known as Log4j, to gain initial access and implant loader malware. Once inside the network, the threat actors were observed moving laterally, escalating their privileges, and eventually gaining access to a disaster recovery network. Sensitive data was collected and exfiltrated during this intrusion.

Upon investigation, indicators of compromise (IOCs) were identified, providing valuable insights into the actions and behavior of the threat actors. These IOCs will aid in future threat detection and response efforts.

The impact of this attack underscores the importance of promptly addressing known vulnerabilities. In this instance, organizations that had not updated their VMware Horizon and UAG systems to the latest versions were vulnerable to attack.

To mitigate the risks associated with this incident, affected organizations are advised to install the fixed builds and update all affected systems to the latest versions. Additionally, it is recommended to minimize the internet-facing attack surface, host essential services on a segregated demilitarized (DMZ) zone, and implement regularly updated web application firewalls (WAFs) in front of public-facing services.

This incident serves as a reminder of the ongoing need for vigilance and proactive cybersecurity measures. Organizations are encouraged to stay informed about emerging threats and vulnerabilities, and to take appropriate steps to protect their systems and data.

In December 2021, state-sponsored Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) actors launched a series of cyber attacks. The targeted organizations possessed affected systems, specifically unpatched, public-facing VMware Horizon and Unified Access Gateway (UAG) servers, which were exploited via the Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228).

Upon exploitation, the APT actors gained initial access and implanted loader malware. Subsequently, they moved laterally within the network, escalated privileges, and accessed a disaster recovery network, ultimately collecting and exfiltrating sensitive data.

Investigations led to the identification of indicators of compromise (IOCs), offering valuable insights into the actions and behavior of the threat actors. These IOCs will aid in future threat detection and response.

The attack's impact highlights the significance of addressing known vulnerabilities promptly. In this case, organizations that failed to update their VMware Horizon and UAG systems to the latest versions were vulnerable to attack.

To mitigate risks, affected organizations are advised to install the fixed builds and update all affected systems to the latest versions. Additionally, it is recommended to minimize the internet-facing attack surface, host essential services on a segregated demilitarized (DMZ) zone, and implement regularly updated web application firewalls (WAFs) in front of public-facing services.

This incident underscores the ongoing need for vigilance and proactive cybersecurity measures. Organizations are encouraged to remain informed about emerging threats and vulnerabilities, and to take appropriate steps to protect their systems and data.

Title: Internal Threat Bulletin - APT Malware Intrusion Detected in Victim 2's Production Environment

Dear Security Team,

I am writing to bring to your attention a significant cyber threat that has been detected in Victim 2's production environment. The actor involved is identified as Advanced Persistent Threat (APT), and the malware used is a Windows loader containing an embedded remote access tool.

The threat was first observed on late January 2022, with the APT gaining initial access to Victim 2’s production environment. On January 30, 2022, the threat actors used PowerShell scripts to call out to a domain name via HTTP. This activity was followed by bi-directional traffic between Victim 2 and a suspected APT IP address, which was observed by CISA in May 2022.

CISA conducted an onsite incident response engagement in late April 2022. The threat actors have exploited the Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228) as one of the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTTPs) employed. The observed TTTPs include T1056.001 (Microsoft Office Macro), T1059.001 (Living Off the Land), T1071.001 (PowerShell), T1090 (Golden SAML), T1105 (DLL Search Order Hijacking), T1053.005 (PowerShell Empire), and T1573.001 (Data from Local System).

The threat actors have targeted Victim 2, and while the sector affected remains unknown, the indicators of compromise include IP addresses, domain names, and port numbers.

To mitigate this threat, it is crucial to promptly patch VMware Horizon servers to address the Log4Shell vulnerability. We strongly advise all relevant teams to prioritize this patching process to prevent further compromise.

Please remain vigilant and proactive in your security measures. I will keep you updated on any further developments.

Regards,
[Your Name]
[Your Position]

Title: Technical Incident Report - MedusaLocker Ransomware Intrusion

In the span of May 2022, our security systems detected and neutralized an incident involving the MedusaLocker ransomware, a particularly harmful strain of malware known to cybersecurity communities.

The actor behind this incident is identified as MedusaLocker, a group known for their persistent attacks and data encryption tactics. The ransomware, upon infiltration, encrypts the victim's data and leaves a ransom note with instructions for communication.

The intrusion methods employed by MedusaLocker align with two tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) defined by MITRE ATT&CK: T1133 (Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) exploitation) and T1566 (Email phishing and spam email campaigns). This indicates a multi-pronged approach, using both direct network access exploits and social engineering techniques to gain entry.

No specific vulnerabilities, as listed in the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) database, were found to be directly exploited during this incident. However, it is essential to prioritize remediating known exploited vulnerabilities to minimize the risk of future attacks.

The targets or sectors affected by this incident remain unspecified in the available data. It is crucial to maintain heightened vigilance across all sectors, given the indiscriminate nature of ransomware attacks.

In response to this incident, we have implemented several mitigation strategies. Firstly, we have initiated user training programs to recognize and report phishing attempts, as they form a significant part of the attack vector used by MedusaLocker. Secondly, we have enabled and enforced multifactor authentication to strengthen our system's security and make it more difficult for attackers to gain unauthorized access.

The incident serves as a reminder of the ever-evolving threat landscape and the importance of proactive cybersecurity measures. We remain committed to protecting our systems and data from such threats and will continue to enhance our defenses in the face of emerging cyber threats.

Title: Technical Incident Report - Zeppelin Actors' Cyberattacks against Multiple Sectors

The investigation uncovered a series of cyberattacks perpetrated by the Zeppelin actors, targeting various sectors including defense, education, manufacturing, technology, and healthcare, between the years 2019 and June 2022. The malware employed in these attacks consisted of the Zeppelin ransomware and the Vega malware family.

The attackers utilized a set of techniques tracked by the Mitre Att&ck framework, specifically T1133 (Spearphishing Attachment), T1190 (Exploit Public Facing Application), T1566 (Social Engineering Lure), and TA0007 (Initial Access via Phishing Link). These tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) suggest that the Zeppelin actors employed a multi-faceted approach, leveraging phishing emails and exploiting publicly facing applications to gain initial access to targeted systems.

The Zeppelin actors targeted a diverse range of organizations, from defense contractors to educational institutions, manufacturers, technology companies, and healthcare providers. This broad scope indicates a high level of sophistication and intent to cause widespread disruption.

The impact of these attacks was significant, ranging from several thousand dollars to over a million dollars per incident. This wide range suggests that the Zeppelin actors were able to successfully infiltrate systems of varying sizes and complexity, resulting in substantial financial losses.

In response to this threat, several mitigation strategies are recommended. First, it is crucial to prioritize the remediation of known exploited vulnerabilities to minimize the attack surface. Second, user training should be enhanced to improve the ability to recognize and report phishing attempts. Lastly, the implementation and enforcement of multifactor authentication can significantly strengthen the security posture of an organization.

This report serves as a warning to all sectors, emphasizing the importance of vigilance and proactive cybersecurity measures. It is imperative that organizations remain aware of the ongoing threat posed by the Zeppelin actors and take appropriate steps to protect their systems and data.

Title: Internal Threat Bulletin - Malicious Cyber Actor Activity Alert

Dear Security Team,

I am writing to inform you of an elevated threat level due to the identification of malicious cyber actors using the Remcos and Agent Tesla malware in targeted attacks. These malicious tools are known for their capabilities in ransomware and data theft.

The specific industries or sectors targeted in these attacks remain undisclosed at this time. However, it is essential to note that all organizations, regardless of sector, are potential targets.

The malware is primarily spread through phishing emails, infected software downloads, and exploitation of unpatched vulnerabilities. As our current intelligence does not indicate any specific zero-day exploits (CVEs), it is crucial to ensure all software is up-to-date to minimize the risk.

The malware often targets Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) and other potentially risky services. To mitigate this, we recommend securing and monitoring these services closely. Network segmentation can also help to limit the spread of any potential infections.

In addition to technical measures, end-user awareness and training are crucial. Employees should be informed about the risks of clicking suspicious links, downloading unverified software, and providing credentials in response to emails from unknown sources.

It is also recommended to make offline backups of data to ensure business continuity in the event of a ransomware attack. If data is encrypted, having offline backups can significantly reduce the recovery time and potential impact on the organization.

Lastly, the implementation of Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) can provide an additional layer of security, making it more challenging for cyber actors to gain unauthorized access.

Please share this information with all relevant team members and departments. Let's remain vigilant and proactive in our security measures to protect our organization from these threats.

Best Regards,
[Your Name]
[Your Position]

In an urgent cybersecurity advisory, we wish to draw attention to the escalating activities of the cybercriminal group known as Vice Society. This threat actor has been observed utilizing a combination of malware, including Hello Kitty/Five Hands and Zeppelin, in their latest campaign.

The group has shown a propensity for exploiting known vulnerabilities, specifically CVE-2021-1675 and CVE-2021-34527. These vulnerabilities are known to be exploited in various techniques, including T1190 (Living Off the Land), T1047 (Imperial Movement), T1068 (PowerShell), T1053 (Golden Master), T1547.001 (Cobalt Strike Beacon), T1574.002 (DLL Side-Loading), T1036 (PowerShell Empire), T1055 (PortForward), and T1497 (System BCDEdit).

Vice Society is known for employing double extortion tactics, which involve both data theft and ransom demands. Network defenders are strongly advised to implement robust cybersecurity measures to mitigate the risks associated with this group.

To strengthen your defenses, it is imperative to use strong, unique, and complex credentials for all accounts. Regularly patching vulnerabilities, especially those referenced above, is crucial to prevent exploitation. Additionally, monitoring network activity and employing anti-malware software can help detect and deter potential intrusions.

It is essential to stay vigilant and proactive in the face of evolving cyber threats. We recommend keeping up-to-date with the latest threat intelligence and best practices to ensure the protection of your networks and assets.

We urge network defenders to remain diligent and share any relevant information with their organizations and relevant cybersecurity authorities. By working together, we can collectively enhance our defenses against the increasing threats in the cyber domain.

Title: Technical Incident Report - IRGC-Affiliated APT Group Cyberattacks

The ongoing cybersecurity incident, commencing in May 2021, has been traced back to an advanced persistent threat (APT) group affiliated with the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). This group has launched a broad range of targeted attacks against various entities, impacting multiple sectors.

The attack vector utilized by the IRGC-affiliated APT group is not solely reliant on malware but instead leverages exploits in several software systems. Notable vulnerabilities targeted include Fortinet, Microsoft Exchange, and VMware Horizon Log4j. The group's tactics demonstrate a high level of sophistication, adapting to the latest vulnerabilities as they emerge.

The primary objective of the attacks appears to be data extortion, disk encryption, and ransom operations. This has resulted in significant disruption and potential data loss for the affected entities. It is crucial to note that the timeline for these attacks is ongoing, and the threat remains active.

To mitigate the risks posed by this APT group, several measures are recommended. First and foremost, maintaining up-to-date systems and software is essential to prevent exploitation of known vulnerabilities. Priority should be given to remedying vulnerabilities that have been exploited in recent attacks.

Second, the implementation of multi-factor authentication (MFA) strengthens account security and reduces the risk of unauthorized access.

Third, making regular offline backups of data is vital for recovery in the event of a successful attack. This ensures that critical data can be restored without the need for ransom payments to the attackers.

While this report provides an overview of the incident and suggested mitigations, continuous monitoring and vigilance are required to effectively counter the threats posed by the IRGC-affiliated APT group.

This APT group has been conducting a wide-ranging series of targeted cyberattacks against multiple entities, affecting various sectors.

The IRGC-affiliated APT group's methodology involves exploiting vulnerabilities in several software systems rather than relying solely on malware. Notable exploited vulnerabilities include Fortinet, Microsoft Exchange, and VMware Horizon Log4j. The group's tactics demonstrate a high level of sophistication, with a propensity to adapt to the latest vulnerabilities as they emerge.

The primary purpose of these attacks seems to be data extortion, disk encryption, and ransom operations. These activities have caused substantial disruption and potential data loss for the targeted entities. It is important to note that this threat remains active, with the timeline for these attacks spanning from May 2021 and continuing.

To mitigate the risks associated with this APT group, several measures are advised. First, ensuring that systems and software are kept up-to-date is crucial to prevent exploitation of known vulnerabilities. Priority should be given to remediating vulnerabilities that have been exploited in recent attacks.

Second, the enforcement of Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) enhances account security and reduces the risk of unauthorized access.

Third, regular offline backups of data are essential for recovery in the event of a successful attack. This ensures that critical data can be restored without the need for ransom payments to the attackers.

Although this analysis offers an overview of the incident and recommended mitigations, continuous monitoring and vigilance are required for effective defense against the threats posed by the IRGC-affiliated APT group.

These entities have exhibited an increasing interest in targeting Operational Technology/Industrial Control Systems (OT/ICS) assets within the U.S. critical infrastructure sectors.

3. Enforcing strong password policies: Implement complex password requirements and consider implementing multi-factor authentication.
4. Network segmentation: Divide the network into smaller segments to limit the spread of an attack.

1. Conducting regular risk assessments and vulnerability scans.
2. Establishing incident response plans and procedures.
3. Providing cybersecurity awareness training for all employees.
4. Implementing intrusion detection systems and security information and event management (SIEM) solutions.
5. Maintaining strong relationships with information sharing and analysis centers (ISACs/ISAOs) to stay informed about emerging threats and best practices.

We urge network defenders to prioritize these actions to mitigate the risk posed by these advanced threats and protect our critical infrastructure. Please stay vigilant, and if you suspect any malicious activity, report it to your local Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT) or the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). Together, we can safeguard our nation's cybersecurity.

The Iranian state cyber actor group, HomeLand Justice, has been identified as the perpetrator, employing a multi-faceted approach that includes ransomware-style file encryptors, disk wiping malware, and the destructive ZeroCleare malware.

The first signs of this campaign were observed in July 2022, where a destructive cyber attack was launched against the Albanian government. Since then, HomeLand Justice has claimed responsibility for the attack on July 18th, and subsequently posted videos of the cyber attack on their website on the 23rd of July.

From late July to mid-August, social media accounts associated with HomeLand Justice have been actively releasing government information, further indicating the group's continued engagement in this operation. The impact of this attack has been substantial, with websites and services becoming unavailable, and potential data exfiltration taking place.

At this moment, no known CVEs or TTPs have been associated with this campaign. However, network defenders are strongly advised to stay vigilant, strengthen their cybersecurity posture, and implement robust defensive measures.

Unfortunately, at present, there are no known mitigations explicitly linked to this specific threat. However, general best practices for cybersecurity, such as regular software updates, multi-factor authentication, and employee cybersecurity training, can help fortify your defenses against such threats.

We urge all network defenders in the Government sector, and particularly those in Albania, to remain vigilant, closely monitor their networks for any suspicious activity, and promptly report any findings to their respective authorities and CTI teams. Together, we can work towards mitigating the risks posed by these sophisticated cyber threats.

Title: Urgent Threat Alert: Iranian Cyber Actors Resurface with Destructive Attack

In a concerning development, our security team has identified renewed cyber activities from Iranian cyber actors targeting the Government of Albania and a specific victim organization.

The attackers have been observed utilizing a variety of tools, including Mimikatz, LSASS dumping, GoXml.exe, a Disk Wiper tool (cl.exe), and an Advanced Port Scanner (advanced_port_scanner.exe). Approximately twelve months after initial access, connections were made to IP addresses belonging to the victim organization's Virtual Private Network (VPN) appliance. Two months before the destructive cyber attack, actions were initiated that resulted in raw disk drives being wiped.

The impact of these attacks has been significant, with a destructive cyber attack leading to the encryption of files and the wiping of raw disk drives. At this time, no known mitigations have been identified, and we urge all team members to remain vigilant and follow best practices for cybersecurity.

We will continue to monitor this situation closely and will provide updates as more information becomes available. In the meantime, please ensure all systems are updated and secure, and report any suspicious activities immediately.

Title: Iranian Government-Sponsored Cyber Threat: Emergence of Potent Malware

In the ever-evolving landscape of cyber threats, a new strain of malware attributed to the Iranian government has surfaced, posing a significant concern for global cybersecurity. The malware, a hybrid of ransomware-style file encryptor and disk wiper utility, is designed to cause extensive damage to affected systems.

The malware's modus operandi is twofold. It encrypts files on the victim's system, demanding ransom to restore access, similar to common ransomware. However, it also possesses a destructive component that overwrites data on the disk, acting as a disk wiper utility, making recovery even more challenging.

The Iranian government-backed actors behind this malware have been known to use various indicators, including Windows executables, digitally signed certificates, RC4 keys, public RSA keys, and Base64 encoded strings. This diverse arsenal suggests a high level of sophistication and adaptability in their operations.

At this time, no specific targets, sectors, or Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) have been identified. However, the potential for widespread disruption cannot be overlooked, given the destructive nature of the malware.

As of now, there is no known timeline for when or where this malware might be deployed. Given the potential impact, it is crucial for organizations to remain vigilant and implement robust cybersecurity measures. Until more information becomes available, proactive measures such as regular system backups, maintaining updated antivirus software, and educating employees about phishing and social engineering tactics can help mitigate the risks.

Stay tuned for updates as we continue to monitor and analyze this emerging threat. In the meantime, we encourage all organizations to prioritize their cybersecurity posture and stay alert for any suspicious activity.

In the interest of maintaining a secure cyber environment, we are issuing this timely advisory to inform network defenders of a significant and ongoing threat activity that has targeted Defense Industrial Base (DIB) Sector organization’s enterprise network from November 2021 through January 2022.

The threat actors involved in this activity are Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) groups, employing tools such as Impacket and CovalentStealer malware in their attacks. APT groups are highly sophisticated, often state-sponsored entities known for their ability to infiltrate and maintain long-term access to targeted networks.

While there have been no reported exploitations of known Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) or Transport Layer Security (TLS) vulnerabilities (TTLS) in this case, network defenders are strongly advised to remain vigilant and maintain up-to-date cyber hygiene practices to reduce the risk of successful attacks.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) associated with this activity are listed below and should be closely monitored by network administrators:

- Impacket malware-related IOCs (IP addresses, domains, MD5 hashes, etc.)
- CovalentStealer malware-related IOCs (IP addresses, domains, MD5 hashes, etc.)

Network defenders are urged to implement appropriate mitigations to protect their systems and networks from these threats. Some potential mitigation strategies include:

- Implementing strong access controls and least privilege principles
- Enforcing multi-factor authentication (MFA) wherever possible
- Regularly patching and updating all systems and applications
- Deploying endpoint detection and response (EDR) solutions to detect and respond to threats in real-time
- Regularly reviewing network logs and intrusion detection systems (IDS) alerts for signs of this activity

By taking proactive measures and staying informed about emerging threats, network defenders can improve their resilience and minimize the risk of a successful cyber attack. We encourage all organizations within the Defense Industrial Base Sector to closely monitor their networks for signs of this activity and take immediate action to address any potential security vulnerabilities.

In an ongoing effort to safeguard critical national infrastructure, we issue this urgent advisory regarding a significant cyber threat targeting Microsoft Exchange servers. The APT (Advanced Persistent Threat) cyber actors have been observed utilizing the CovalentStealer malware in their operations.

The threat actors are leveraging a variety of tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) to infiltrate targeted networks. Notably, they are using Impacket tools, specifically wmiexec.py and smbexec.py, to exploit the Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) and Server Message Block (SMB) protocols.

Furthermore, these actors have been observed utilizing virtual private network (VPN) and virtual private server (VPS) providers to mask their activities. They also employ Outlook Web Access (OWA) and PowerShell commands for managing Exchange servers in their attacks.

Network defenders are strongly advised to be vigilant against these TTPs. Particular attention should be paid to the following indicators of compromise: IP addresses, domain names, file paths, and user credentials.

While the specific timeline of this activity is not clearly defined, it underscores the need for continuous vigilance and proactive defense measures.

To mitigate this threat, we recommend implementing the following measures:

1. Regularly update and patch all systems, focusing on Microsoft Exchange servers.
2. Restrict the use of Impacket tools, WMI, SMB, VPN, VPS, OWA, and PowerShell within your network to authorized users and systems.
3. Implement robust network segmentation and access controls to limit the spread of potential malware.
4. Utilize intrusion detection and prevention systems to monitor for suspicious activity.
5. Strengthen password policies and enforce multi-factor authentication wherever possible.
6. Educate users about phishing and social engineering tactics to avoid inadvertently aiding cyber actors.

Stay vigilant, and remember that your continued efforts in cybersecurity defense are crucial in safeguarding our nation's digital infrastructure.

Title: Technical Incident Report - Unauthenticated Actor Exploitation of Unpatched F5 BIG-IP Devices

Incident Summary:
An unauthenticated actor has been identified as leveraging the known vulnerability CVE-2022-1388 to gain control over unpatched F5 BIG-IP devices. This incident affects both government and private sector entities, increasing the potential impact and scope of the exploitation.

Timeline of Events:
- May 4, 2022: F5 released patches to address the CVE-2022-1388 vulnerability.
- Following the patch release, publicly available proof of concept (POC) exploits were released, allowing malicious actors to easily exploit the vulnerability.

Targets and Sectors Affected:
The targets of this exploit are unpatched F5 BIG-IP devices, which are widely used in both government and private sector organizations.

Impact of the Incident:
The exploitation of this vulnerability allows the actor to gain control of affected systems, potentially leading to widespread disruptions in the targeted organizations.

Indicators and Mitigations:
No specific indicators of compromise or types have been identified at this time. However, the following mitigations are recommended to address this incident:
- Upgrading software to the fixed versions released by F5 to eliminate the vulnerability.
- Deploying detection signatures to identify any attempts to exploit the vulnerability within the network.
- Applying incident response recommendations, such as conducting a thorough network assessment, isolating compromised systems, and implementing recovery procedures as needed.

Continuous monitoring and vigilance are essential in preventing further exploitation and minimizing potential damage. Organizations are advised to prioritize patching and implementing security measures to protect against similar incidents.

The vulnerability exploited in this instance is CVE-2022-1388, a security flaw that was publicly disclosed on May 4, 2022, and was later added to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog on May 11, 2022, indicating its potential severity and wide-ranging impact.

The exploitation of this vulnerability allows the attacker to execute arbitrary system commands, create or delete files, or disable services, thereby compromising the integrity, confidentiality, and availability of affected systems. As of now, there is no reported public release of Proof-of-Concept (POC) exploits associated with this vulnerability.

The incident response team recommends immediate action to mitigate the threat. Organizations affected by this incident should apply the available patch as soon as possible. Additionally, it is advisable to refer to CISA’s Federal Government Cybersecurity Incident and Vulnerability Response Playbooks for comprehensive guidance.

For added protection, a joint Cybersecurity Advisory has been issued by the cybersecurity authorities of Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States. It is strongly recommended to review and implement the measures outlined in this advisory to fortify defenses against this ongoing threat.

As of now, there is no reported public release of Proof-of-Concept (POC) exploits associated with this vulnerability.

To mitigate the threat, organizations should immediately apply the available patch. Additionally, refer to CISA’s Federal Government Cybersecurity Incident and Vulnerability Response Playbooks for comprehensive guidance. For additional protection, review and implement the measures outlined in the joint Cybersecurity Advisory issued by the cybersecurity authorities of Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and the United States.

Title: Internal Threat Bulletin - Daixin Actor Targeting HPH Sector via Babuk Locker Malware

The Security Operations Center (SOC) team is issuing a threat bulletin regarding a potential cyber attack targeting the HPH sector. The actor, identified as Daixin, is employing the Babuk Locker ransomware in these attacks.

Daixin has been observed utilizing a series of tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) in these attacks, including SSH, RDP, Rclone, Ngrok, and others. The specific TTPs used are enumerated as follows: T1563.001, T1563.002, T1003, T1550.002, T1098, T1486, TA0010, and T1567.

The primary targets of these attacks are ESXi servers, and data exfiltration and ransomware deployment have been noted as the impact of these attacks. It is essential to emphasize that no CVEs have been associated with this threat at this time.

The SOC team strongly recommends the following mitigations to fortify your organization's security posture:

1. Implement secure account management practices, such as strong password policies and multi-factor authentication.
2. Regularly update and patch systems to protect against known vulnerabilities.
3. Monitor for suspicious activity, both internally and externally, to detect any potential intrusions early.
4. Use secure protocols for remote access, such as VPNs, to minimize exposure.
5. Implement data backup and recovery procedures to ensure business continuity in the event of a successful attack.

Remember, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. By implementing these mitigations, your organization can significantly reduce its risk of falling victim to the Daixin actor and the Babuk Locker ransomware.

The SOC team will continue to monitor this threat and provide updates as new information becomes available. In the meantime, remain vigilant and proactive in your cybersecurity efforts.

Title: Technical Incident Report - Daixin Team Ransomware Attack on U.S. Businesses in the Healthcare Sector

This report details an ongoing cyber incident involving the Daixin Team and their deployment of ransomware, primarily targeting U.S. businesses within the Healthcare and Public Health (HPH) sector.

The Daixin Team, a known advanced persistent threat (APT) group, has been active since at least June 2022. Their latest campaign has seen the deployment of ransomware, a destructive malware designed to encrypt data and demand ransom for its decryption.

The TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) associated with this incident include:
- Initial Access (T1190) - This suggests the Daixin Team may have exploited known vulnerabilities or gained access through compromised credentials.
- Command and Control (T1078) - The use of external remote services for C2 purposes.
- Lateral Movement (T1598.002) - Indicates the malware has the ability to move within the targeted network, potentially compromising multiple systems.

The targets of this attack have primarily been businesses in the HPH sector, a crucial area with sensitive data that, if compromised, could have severe consequences.

This incident is significant due to the use of ransomware, the targeted sector, and the TTPs associated with the Daixin Team. As such, it is crucial for organizations within the HPH sector to be vigilant and implement appropriate security measures.

Currently, there are no reported impacts or mitigations associated with this incident. However, it is recommended that affected organizations:
1. Review their network for any IOCs (Indicators of Compromise) associated with the Daixin Team.
2. Strengthen their security posture by implementing multi-factor authentication, patch management, and regular security audits.
3. If an incident is suspected, promptly engage cybersecurity professionals to assist in response and recovery efforts.

Further investigation is ongoing to determine the extent and full impact of this attack, as well as to identify any additional IOCs that may aid in detection and response efforts.

Title: Incident Report - APT Actor Intrusion in FCEB Network (mid-June to mid-July 2022)

In the period from mid-June to mid-July 2022, an Iranian government-sponsored Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) actor infiltrated the Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) organization's network.

The actor exploited the Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE) to gain initial access, subsequently installing XMRig crypto mining software on several hosts for malicious crypto mining activities. Additionally, the APT actor moved laterally to the domain controller (DC), compromising credentials and implanting Ngrok reverse proxies on multiple hosts.

Throughout this intrusion, the threat actor displayed TTPs (Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures) consistent with a sophisticated APT group. The identified IOCs (Indicators of Compromise) related to this incident include the specific XMRig crypto mining software variants and Ngrok reverse proxies' unique configurations used during the attack.

The compromise of the FCEB network resulted in the exposure of sensitive information and potential disruption of services within the targeted sectors (FCEB). Immediate actions to mitigate the ongoing threat included applying available patches or workarounds for the exploited Log4Shell vulnerability, initiating threat hunting activities, assuming lateral movement by the threat actors, investigating connected systems (including the DC), and auditing privileged accounts.

Further efforts are underway to clean affected systems, secure vulnerable services, and strengthen the network's overall security posture to prevent future incursions. A detailed post-incident analysis will be conducted to determine the initial vector of attack, identify any potential data breaches, and develop strategies to enhance the organization's defense mechanisms.

Title: Unveiling Recent Tactics by Persistent Threat Actors: A Closer Look at Mimikatz and Ngrok

In the ever-evolving cybersecurity landscape, it's crucial to stay informed about the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) employed by threat actors. Recently, we've observed a significant surge in the use of two tools, Mimikatz and Ngrok, by these malicious actors.

Mimikatz, a renowned post-exploitation tool, is used for extracting credentials from the volatile memory of compromised systems. Its ability to bypass security measures makes it a preferred choice among threat actors. On the other hand, Ngrok, a tunneling software, is used to create secure, public tunnels to local servers, enabling remote access and potential lateral movement within networks.

The threat actors are leveraging TTPs such as T1136.002 (Living off the Land), T1090 (Actively Exploited), T1018 (PowerShell), T1098 (Command and Scripting Interpreter), and T1003.001 (Screen Capture) to execute their attacks. The use of these TTPs indicates a high level of sophistication and persistence in their operations.

While we don't have specific CVEs associated with these incidents, it underscores the importance of maintaining up-to-date system patches and strengthening overall security posture.

In response to this threat, we recommend implementing additional anti-virus measures, changing passwords for local administrator accounts, and closely monitoring for signs of lateral movement within your network. By taking these steps, you can significantly reduce the risk of falling victim to these advanced tactics employed by threat actors.

Stay vigilant and keep your defenses strong. We will continue to monitor this situation and provide updates as new information becomes available.

Recipients: SOC Team, IT Security, Incident Response, and Threat Intelligence

**Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs)**

The threat actor utilized Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP, T1021.001) to gain initial access. Default accounts (T1078.001) and lateral movement techniques (TA0008) were employed to navigate within the network.

The Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228) was exploited to facilitate the attack. This vulnerability, if not properly patched, can allow remote code execution on affected systems.

**Mitigations**

No specific mitigations were mentioned in the excerpt, but it is strongly recommended to ensure all systems are patched against the Log4Shell vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228), implement secure RDP configurations, and regularly review system logs for signs of unauthorized activity.

**Recommendations**

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) is issuing this advisory to notify network defenders of ongoing activity by the Hive ransomware actors. Since June 2021, these cybercriminals have targeted a wide range of businesses and critical infrastructure sectors, including Government Facilities, Communications, Critical Manufacturing, Information Technology, Healthcare and Public Health (HPH).

Over the course of the past year, Hive ransomware actors have reportedly compromised over 1,300 companies worldwide, resulting in approximately US$100 million in ransom payments. This alarming trend underscores the need for enhanced cybersecurity measures to protect against these malicious actors.

Although the specific vulnerabilities exploited by Hive ransomware (CVEs) are currently unknown, the multi-sector nature of the attacks underscores the need for robust network security practices. Organizations in the affected sectors are urged to review and strengthen their security posture to mitigate the risk of compromise.

Network defenders are strongly advised to implement the following protective measures:

1. Implement multiple layers of defense, including network segmentation, multi-factor authentication, and least privilege access.
2. Regularly update and patch systems to reduce the likelihood of exploitation by known vulnerabilities.
3. Deploy email and web filtering to block malicious content, particularly email attachments and links from unknown or untrusted sources.
4. Employ threat hunting and security information and event management (SIEM) solutions to detect anomalous behavior.
5. Regularly back up data and verify its integrity, ensuring it can be rapidly restored in the event of a compromise.
6. Establish a response plan that includes incident response teams, communication plans, and procedures for reporting incidents to law enforcement and CISA.

Stay vigilant and remain informed of the latest threats. For more information about the Hive ransomware and other cyber threats, visit https://www.cisa.gov/rumorcontrol. To report a cyber incident, contact the CISA 24/7 watchcenter at https://us-cert.cisa.gov/report.

Incident Report: Cyber Intrusion by Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) Actor

The investigation has identified an ongoing cyber intrusion by an Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) actor, which began on January 6, 2021, and continued until January 25, 2021. The threat actor has targeted federal, state, and local governments, critical infrastructure entities, and private sector organizations across various sectors.

The attack aimed to gain access to and privileges over highly sensitive information, potentially compromising the security and integrity of affected systems. The specific malware or Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) exploited during this incident remain undetermined at this time.

Temporal analysis of the incident reveals that the initial compromise occurred on January 6, 2021, with subsequent activities observed on January 19, 2021, and January 25, 2021. The APT actor appears to have used Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) to maintain persistence and evade detection.

To mitigate the ongoing threat, the following actions have been implemented:
1. Forensic analysis is ongoing to determine the scope and extent of the breach, as well as to identify the tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) used by the APT actor.
2. Hardening requirements have been implemented to strengthen the security posture of affected systems and reduce the likelihood of future intrusions.
3. Collaboration with the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) Hunt and Incident Response Program (CHIRP) has been initiated to ensure comprehensive and coordinated response efforts.

It is essential that affected organizations remain vigilant and closely monitor their networks for any signs of continued activity by the APT actor. Further updates will be provided as the investigation continues to progress.

Title: Technical Incident Report - CovalentStealer Infiltration

In the recent security event, the organization has experienced an infiltration by the malware known as CovalentStealer. The actor responsible for the attack remains unknown at this time.

Upon investigation, the malicious agent was identified as an obfuscated .NET executable, a common tactic used by threat actors to evade detection. The malware was found to be carrying an encrypted configuration file, which is a characteristic feature of CovalentStealer.

During the course of the intrusion, the threat actor managed to obtain a refresh token for an OAuth client. This token, while not the primary access credential, can potentially be used for continuous access to the compromised systems or services.

Furthermore, the incident has led to the theft of sensitive credential information. The exact nature and extent of this data breach are still under evaluation, but it is evident that the threat actor has gained unauthorized access to valuable data.

Another critical indicator is the IP address of the server the malware communicated with. This information will be instrumental in tracking the actor's origin and potential associates.

At present, the timeline of the incident is unclear, and a thorough analysis is required to determine the initial point of entry and the duration of the intrusion.

The impact of this incident is currently being assessed, but it is apparent that the organization's security has been compromised, and sensitive data may have been exposed.

Immediate mitigation steps include isolating affected systems, revoking and resetting all OAuth tokens, and implementing strengthened authentication measures. The organization's IT department is also working on decrypting the malware's configuration file to gain further insights into the attack.

A full incident response plan is being developed in collaboration with cybersecurity experts to prevent future occurrences and minimize the potential damage from this incident. Further updates will be provided as the investigation progresses.

This report details the recent infiltration of the organization by the malware, CovalentStealer. The perpetrator behind the attack remains unknown.

Upon investigation, the malicious agent was identified as an obfuscated .NET executable, a tactic frequently employed by threat actors to avoid detection. The malware was found to contain an encrypted configuration file, a characteristic feature of CovalentStealer.

During the intrusion, the threat actor acquired a refresh token for an OAuth client. While not a primary access credential, this token could potentially grant continuous access to compromised systems or services.

The incident resulted in the theft of sensitive credential information. The magnitude and specifics of the data breach are still being evaluated, but it's clear that the threat actor gained unauthorized access to valuable data.

A critical indicator is the IP address of the server the malware communicated with, which will aid in tracking the actor's origin and potential associates.

The timeline of the incident is yet to be established, requiring a comprehensive analysis to determine the initial point of entry and the duration of the intrusion.

The impact of this incident is being assessed, but it's evident that the organization's security has been breached, and sensitive data may have been exposed.

Immediate mitigation steps include isolating affected systems, revoking and resetting all OAuth tokens, and implementing strengthened authentication measures. The organization's IT department is also working on decrypting the malware's configuration file to gain further insights into the attack.

A comprehensive incident response plan, in collaboration with cybersecurity experts, is being developed to prevent future occurrences and minimize potential damage from this incident. Further updates will be provided as the investigation progresses.

While specific threat actors remain elusive in our recent analysis, we've identified a concerning rise in the use of certain tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) by various threat groups.

Title: APT Actors Target Defense Industrial Base with Modified China Chopper Malware

In the rapidly evolving cyber threat landscape, a new concern has emerged for organizations within the Defense Industrial Base (DIB) Sector. Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) actors have been identified as leveraging the China Chopper malware in an attempt to infiltrate DIB targets.

The malicious campaign, while not linked to any specific Critical Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) or Transport Layer Security (TLS) vulnerabilities (TTLS), is executed through modified Offline Address Book (OAB) Virtual Directory (VD) configuration files, the ExternalUrl parameter, and JavaScript code.

The impact of this attack is significant, enabling unauthorized access for dynamic remote code execution against Exchange servers. This breach poses a potential threat to sensitive data within the defense sector, underscoring the need for increased vigilance and proactive security measures.

At present, there are no known mitigations for this specific attack. However, awareness of the indicators associated with this threat—modified OAB VD configuration files, the ExternalUrl parameter, and JavaScript code—can help organizations detect and respond more effectively.

As the threat continues to evolve, it is crucial for organizations to stay informed and vigilant, reinforcing their cyber defenses to protect against such targeted attacks. The security community must work together to counteract these threats and ensure the continued safety and security of sensitive data in the defense sector.

Excerpt: New vulnerabilities are continually emerging, but the best defense against attackers exploiting patched vulnerabilities is simple: keep software up to date. Timely patching is one of the most efficient and cost-effective steps an organization can take to minimize its exposure to cybersecurity threats. On January 14, 2020, Microsoft released software fixes to address 49 vulnerabilities as part of their monthly Patch Tuesday announcement. Among the vulnerabilities patched were critical weaknesses in Windows CryptoAPI, Windows Remote Desktop Gateway (RD Gateway), and Windows Remote Desktop Client. An attacker could remotely exploit these vulnerabilities to decrypt, modify, or inject data on user connections: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) is unaware of active exploitation of these vulnerabilities. However, because patches have been publicly released, the underlying vulnerabilities can be reverse-engineered to create exploits that target unpatched systems. CISA strongly recommends organizations install these critical patches as soon as possible—prioritize patching by starting with mission critical systems, internet-facing systems, and networked servers. Organizations should then prioritize patching other affected information technology/operational technology (IT/OT) assets. According to Microsoft, “an attacker could exploit the vulnerability by using a spoofed code-signing certificate to sign a malicious executable, making it appear the file was from a trusted, legitimate source. The user would have no way of knowing the file was malicious, because the digital signature would appear to be from a trusted provider.” Additionally, “a successful exploit could also allow the attacker to conduct man-in-the-middle attacks and decrypt confidential information on user connections to the affected software.” A cyber attacker could exploit CVE-2020-0601 to obtain sensitive information, such as financial information, or run malware on a targeted system; for example: The National Security Agency (NSA) provides detection measures for CVE-2020-0601 in their Cybersecurity Advisory: Patch Critical Cryptographic Vulnerability in Microsoft Windows Clients and Servers . According to Microsoft, “A remote code execution vulnerability exists in Windows Remote Desktop Gateway (RD Gateway) when an unauthenticated attacker connects to the target system using RDP and sends specially crafted requests. This vulnerability is pre-authentication and requires no user interaction.” ,

In the ever-evolving landscape of cyber threats, maintaining up-to-date software is a crucial defense mechanism against attackers exploiting previously patched vulnerabilities. Timely patching is a highly effective and cost-efficient strategy for minimizing an organization's vulnerability to cybersecurity risks. On January 14, 2020, as part of their regular Patch Tuesday announcements, Microsoft issued software updates to address 49 identified vulnerabilities. Among these were critical flaws in Windows CryptoAPI, Windows Remote Desktop Gateway (RD Gateway), and Windows Remote Desktop Client. These vulnerabilities could potentially allow an attacker to decrypt, manipulate, or inject data during user connections, despite CISA's current lack of knowledge about active exploitation.

However, since patches have been made public, there's a risk that these vulnerabilities could be reverse-engineered to create exploits for unpatched systems. Therefore, CISA strongly advises organizations to install these critical patches as soon as possible. It's recommended to prioritize patching mission-critical systems, internet-facing systems, and networked servers first, followed by other affected IT/OT assets.

Microsoft has warned that an attacker could exploit these vulnerabilities by using a counterfeit code-signing certificate to make a malicious executable appear trustworthy. This would make it difficult for users to distinguish between legitimate and harmful files. A successful exploit could also enable the attacker to carry out man-in-the-middle attacks and decrypt confidential information on user connections to the affected software.

An attacker could leverage CVE-2020-0601 to obtain sensitive information, such as financial details, or run malware on a targeted system. For instance, the National Security Agency (NSA) has provided detection measures for CVE-2020-0601 in their Cybersecurity Advisory: Patch Critical Cryptographic Vulnerability in Microsoft Windows Clients and Servers.

Additionally, Microsoft has disclosed a remote code execution vulnerability in Windows Remote Desktop Gateway (RD Gateway). This vulnerability occurs when an unauthenticated attacker connects to the target system using RDP and sends specially crafted requests. This vulnerability is pre-authentication and requires no user interaction.

Excerpt: This is a joint alert from the United States Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC). CISA and NCSC continue to see indications that advanced persistent threat (APT) groups are exploiting the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic as part of their cyber operations. This joint alert highlights ongoing activity by APT groups against organizations involved in both national and international COVID-19 responses. It describes some of the methods these actors are using to target organizations and provides mitigation advice. The joint CISA-NCSC Alert: (AA20-099A) COVID-19 Exploited by Malicious Cyber Actors from April 8, 2020, previously detailed the exploitation of the COVID-19 pandemic by cybercriminals and APT groups. This joint CISA-NCSC Alert provides an update to ongoing malicious cyber activity relating to COVID-19. For a graphical summary of CISA’s joint COVID-19 Alerts with NCSC, see the following guide . APT actors are actively targeting organizations involved in both national and international COVID-19 responses. These organizations include healthcare bodies, pharmaceutical companies, academia, medical research organizations, and local governments. APT actors frequently target organizations in order to collect bulk personal information, intellectual property, and intelligence that aligns with national priorities. The pandemic has likely raised additional interest for APT actors to gather information related to COVID-19. For example, actors may seek to obtain intelligence on national and international healthcare policy or acquire sensitive data on COVID-19-related research. Cyber Threat Intelligence Report: Password Spraying Attacks Targeting Organizations

In recent investigations, malicious cyber actors have employed password spraying techniques to infiltrate corporate email accounts within organizations. Once access is gained, these actors leverage the compromised accounts to download the Global Address List (GAL). Subsequently, they use the GAL to execute further password spray attacks, aiming to access additional accounts and networks.

Attackers frequently utilize predictable passwords in password spray attacks, such as those based on the month of the year, seasons, and company or organization names. The ongoing investigation suggests a significant increase in large-scale password spraying campaigns, with Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) actors exploiting the COVID-19 pandemic to gather intelligence related to the crisis.

In response to this heightened activity, CISA and NCSC advise organizations to implement the following mitigation measures:

1. Enhance password policies by using complex and unique passwords, avoiding commonly used passwords.
2. Regularly update and monitor accounts for suspicious activity.
3. Implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) where possible to add an extra layer of security.
4. Educate employees about the risks of phishing and other social engineering tactics.

CISA and NCSC have previously published resources on password spraying prevention and password policy improvement. Implementing these recommendations will substantially decrease the likelihood of compromise from such attacks.

CISA's Cyber Essentials for small organizations offers guiding principles for leaders to cultivate a security-focused culture and provides specific actions for IT professionals to put this culture into practice. Additionally, the UK government's Cyber Aware campaign offers valuable advice for individuals on how to maintain online security during the coronavirus pandemic. This includes recommendations on protecting passwords, accounts, and devices.

This report is based on information sourced from CISA, NCSC, and industry sources. The findings and recommendations are not intended to eliminate all risks; following them will merely reduce the risk level. It is important to note that ownership of information risks remains with the relevant system owner at all times.

Excerpt: This Activity Alert provides an overview of the threat posed by each tool, along with insight into where and when it has been deployed by threat actors. Measures to aid detection and limit the effectiveness of each tool are also described. First observed in May 2015, the JBiFrost RAT is a variant of the Adwind RAT, with roots stretching back to the Frutas RAT from 2012. A RAT is a program that, once installed on a victim’s machine, allows remote administrative control. In a malicious context, it can—among many other functions—be used to install backdoors and key loggers, take screen shots, and exfiltrate data. Malicious RATs can be difficult to detect because they are normally designed not to appear in lists of running programs and can mimic the behavior of legitimate applications. To prevent forensic analysis, RATs have been known to disable security measures (e.g., Task Manager) and network analysis tools (e.g., Wireshark) on the victim’s system. JBiFrost RAT is typically employed by cyber criminals and low-skilled threat actors, but its capabilities could easily be adapted for use by state-sponsored threat actors. Other RATs are widely used by Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) actor groups, such as Adwind RAT, against the aerospace and defense sector; or Quasar RAT, by APT10, against a broad range of sectors. Threat actors have repeatedly compromised servers in our countries with the purpose of delivering malicious RATs to victims, either to gain remote access for further exploitation, or to steal valuable information such as banking credentials, intellectual property, or PII. JBiFrost RAT allows threat actors to pivot and move laterally across a network or install additional malicious software. It is primarily delivered through emails as an attachment, usually an invoice notice, request for quotation, remittance notice, shipment notification, payment notice, or with a link to a file hosting service. Past infections have exfiltrated intellectual property, banking credentials, and personally identifiable information (PII). Machines infected with JBiFrost RAT can also be used in botnets to carry out distributed denial-of-service attacks.

Excerpt: Since early 2018, we have observed an increase in JBiFrost RAT being used in targeted attacks against critical national infrastructure owners and their supply chain operators. There has also been an increase in the RAT’s hosting on infrastructure located in our countries. In early 2017, Adwind RAT was deployed via spoofed emails designed to look as if they originated from Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication, or SWIFT, network services. Many other publicly available RATs, including variations of Gh0st RAT, have also been observed in use against a range of victims worldwide. Protection is best afforded by ensuring systems and installed applications are all fully patched and updated. The use of a modern antivirus program with automatic definition updates and regular system scans will also help ensure that most of the latest variants are stopped in their tracks. You should ensure that your organization is able to collect antivirus detections centrally across its estate and investigate RAT detections efficiently. The initial infection mechanism for RATs, including JBiFrost RAT, can be via phishing emails. You can help prevent JBiFrost RAT infections by stopping these phishing emails from reaching your users, helping users to identify and report phishing emails, and implementing security controls so that the malicious email does not compromise your device. The United Kingdom National Cyber Security Centre (UK NCSC) has published phishing guidance . Webshells are malicious scripts that are uploaded to a target host after an initial compromise and grant a threat actor remote administrative capability. China Chopper is extensively used by threat actors to remotely access compromised web servers, where it provides file and directory management, along with access to a virtual terminal on the compromised device. As China Chopper is just 4 KB in size and has an easily modifiable payload, detection and mitigation are difficult for network defenders. China Chopper has two main components: the China Chopper client-side, which is run by the attacker, and the China Chopper server, which is installed on the victim web server but is also attacker-controlled.

Additionally, there's been a noticeable rise in the trojan's presence on infrastructure within our jurisdictions.

In the opening months of 2017, the Adwind RAT was deployed through deceptive emails that mimicked Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) network services. Multiple other publicly accessible RATs, including altered versions of Gh0st RAT, have also been found being used against a diverse array of global targets.

Effective protection can be achieved by ensuring all systems and software are consistently patched and updated. Installing a contemporary antivirus program that updates definitions automatically and conducts regular system scans will also be beneficial in thwarting many of the latest variants. Organizations should strive to collect antivirus detections centrally across their entire network and investigate RAT detections in an efficient manner.

The initial infection vector for RATs, including JBiFrost RAT, often originates from phishing emails. To prevent JBiFrost RAT infections, efforts should be made to stop these phishing emails from reaching users, assist users in identifying and reporting phishing emails, and implement security measures to ensure that the malicious email does not compromise the device.

The United Kingdom National Cyber Security Centre (UK NCSC) has published guidance on phishing prevention. Another malicious tool frequently used by threat actors is the Webshell, malicious scripts uploaded to a target host post-initial compromise, providing a threat actor with remote administrative privileges. China Chopper is one such Webshell, widely used to access compromised web servers. It offers file and directory management, along with a virtual terminal on the compromised device.

Due to its small size (4 KB) and easily modifiable payload, China Chopper is challenging for network defenders to detect and mitigate. China Chopper consists of two primary components: the China Chopper client-side, run by the attacker, and the China Chopper server, installed on the victim web server but controlled by the attacker as well.

Title: Analysis of Chinese State-Sponsored Cyber Threats and Mitigation Strategies

The U.S. Intelligence Community, along with numerous private sector threat intelligence organizations, have identified the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) and Ministry of State Security (MSS) as key instigators of state-sponsored cyberattacks. These entities, either directly or through contractors in the Chinese private sector, are involved in espionage activities aimed at stealing sensitive data such as innovation capital, intellectual property (IP), and personally identifiable information (PII). China has shown a propensity to extend the scope of these activities to acquire information crucial for boosting their economic standing and competitive edge.

Evidence from multiple Department of Justice (DOJ) indictments over the years indicates that Chinese threat actors persistently aim to illegally obtain and exfiltrate U.S. IP, with targets also extending to western companies operating within China.

The following section outlines common tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) employed by Chinese threat actors, which align with the MITRE ATT&CK framework. Where applicable, detection and mitigation actions are provided. It's important to note that this list is not exhaustive and does not cover all TTPs or detection and mitigation methods.

Chinese threat actors frequently utilize publicly known TTPs against enterprise networks. To execute attacks, they employ commonly used security testing tools and methodologies, as detailed in Table 2.

**Table 2: Common TTPs Used by Chinese Threat Actors Against Enterprise Networks**

| Tactic | Technique | Detection & Mitigation |
|--------|-----------|----------------------|
| Initial Access | Spearphishing | Implement email filtering and user awareness training |
| Initial Access | Exploit Public-Facing Applications | Regularly update and patch all applications |
| Defense Evasion | Living off the Land | Monitor system processes for unusual behavior |
| Credential Access | Password Spraying | Implement multi-factor authentication and least privilege principles |
| Lateral Movement | Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) Abuse | Regularly audit and secure RDP connections |
| Exfiltration | Data Compression | Monitor network traffic for unusual data compression |

While the mitigations mentioned in this alert can help reduce vulnerability to these TTPs, it's crucial for defenders to remain vigilant against threat actors who innovate their approach, making it challenging to detect and respond to compromise.

In addition, the following actionable technical recommendations can help IT security professionals reduce their organization's overall vulnerability:

1. Regularly update and patch all systems and applications.
2. Implement email filtering and user awareness training.
3. Monitor system processes for unusual behavior.
4. Implement multi-factor authentication and least privilege principles.
5. Regularly audit and secure Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) connections.
6. Monitor network traffic for unusual data compression.

These recommendations focus on actions that significantly reduce the attack surface, but they are not exhaustive.

Excerpt: The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has consistently observed Chinese Ministry of State Security (MSS)-affiliated cyber threat actors using publicly available information sources and common, well-known tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs) to target U.S. Government agencies. CISA has observed these—and other threat actors with varying degrees of skill—routinely using open-source information to plan and execute cyber operations. CISA leveraged the MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK®) and Pre-ATT&CK frameworks to characterize the TTPs used by Chinese MSS-affiliated actors. This product was written by CISA with contributions by the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). Through the operation of the National Cybersecurity Protection System (NCPS) and by fulfilling its mission as the national risk advisor, CISA has observed Chinese MSS-affiliated cyber threat actors operating from the People’s Republic of China using commercially available information sources and open-source exploitation tools to target U.S. Government agency networks. According to a recent U.S. Department of Justice indictment, MSS-affiliated actors have targeted various industries across the United States and other countries—including high-tech manufacturing; medical device, civil, and industrial engineering; business, educational, and gaming software; solar energy; pharmaceuticals; and defense—in a campaign that lasted over ten years. These hackers acted for both their own personal gain and the benefit of the Chinese MSS. To conceal the theft of information from victim networks and otherwise evade detection, the defendants typically packaged victim data in encrypted Roshal Archive Compressed files (RAR files), changed RAR file and victim documents’ names and extensions (e.g., from “.rar” to “.jpg”) and system timestamps, and concealed programs and documents at innocuous-seeming locations on victim networks and in victim networks’ “recycle bins.” The defendants frequently returned to re-victimize companies, government entities, and organizations from which they had previously stolen data, in some cases years after the initial successful data theft. In several instances, however, the defendants were unsuccessful in this regard, due to the efforts of the FBI and network defenders.

To better understand these TTPs, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has utilized the MITRE Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge (ATT&CK®) and Pre-ATT&CK frameworks. This analysis, which was collaboratively produced by CISA and the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), reveals that MSS-affiliated actors have been found to operate from within the People's Republic of China, using commercially available information sources and open-source exploitation tools to infiltrate U.S. Government agency networks.

According to a recent U.S. Department of Justice indictment, MSS-affiliated actors have been targeting various industries across the United States and other countries for over a decade. These industries include high-tech manufacturing, medical device and industrial engineering, software development, solar energy, pharmaceuticals, and defense sectors. The hackers were motivated both by personal gain and the interests of the Chinese MSS.

To conceal their activities and evade detection, the attackers often encrypt the stolen data within Roshal Archive Compressed files (RAR files), rename these files and associated documents, and alter system timestamps. They also hide programs and documents in seemingly harmless locations within the victim networks or in their "recycle bins." In some cases, these actors have returned to re-target companies, government entities, and organizations from which they had previously stolen data, sometimes years after the initial intrusion. However, in several instances, their efforts have been thwarted due to the combined efforts of the FBI and network defenders.
